# Jollof Rice 🇳🇬

::: {.dish-meta}
**Region:** West Africa (Nigeria, Ghana, Senegal & beyond)  ·  **Family:** One-pot pilaf
**Serves:** 6  ·  **Active time:** 45 minutes  ·  **Total:** 1 hour 15 min
**Assembly:** 🍲🍽️ Hybrid — one-pot rice; chicken browned separately and folded in
:::

Deep red, smoky, and gently fiery, jollof is the beating heart of West African
celebration cooking — and the subject of the internet's most joyful rivalry, the
"Jollof Wars," in which Nigeria and Ghana each insist theirs is supreme. This is a
Nigerian-leaning version, served with chicken.

## The story

Jollof traces to the **Wolof people** of the Senegambia region, whose dish
*thieboudienne* (*ceebu jën*) — rice cooked in a rich tomato-and-fish stew — is
widely considered its ancestor. As the technique spread across West Africa it
took on local character everywhere it landed: Senegalese versions lean on fish
and broken rice, Ghanaian cooks favor aromatic jasmine or basmati, and Nigerians
build a long-simmered pepper base and chase the prized **"party jollof"** flavor —
that faint, irresistible smokiness from rice caught and toasted at the bottom of
a big pot over open flame.

## Ingredients

**The pepper base (the soul of the dish)**

- 3 red bell peppers, roughly chopped
- 2 large tomatoes (or 400 g canned)
- 1–2 scotch bonnet peppers (respect them — start with one)
- 1 large onion

**Everything else**

- 500 g (2.5 cups) parboiled long-grain rice, rinsed well
- 6 chicken pieces (thighs/drumsticks), seasoned and browned or roasted
- 1 onion, sliced
- 4 tbsp tomato paste
- 80 ml (⅓ cup) neutral oil (traditionally more)
- 2 tsp curry powder, 1 tsp dried thyme
- 2 bay leaves, 1 tsp white pepper
- 1 tbsp smoked paprika (for color and, well, smoke)
- ~500 ml (2 cups) chicken stock
- 1 **certified gluten-free, dairy-free** bouillon/seasoning cube (many Maggi/Knorr
  cubes contain wheat and/or milk — check the label), salt

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Gluten-free · dairy-free:** the pepper base, rice, and oil are naturally both.
The one thing to watch is the **seasoning cube** — use a certified GF/DF bouillon
(or just good homemade stock and a little extra salt). Curry powder is usually GF,
but check the blend.
:::

## Method

1. Blend the pepper-base ingredients until smooth. Pour into a pot and **boil it
   down** over medium heat, 12–15 minutes, until reduced and jammy and the raw
   tomato smell is gone. This step is what separates good jollof from sour,
   watery jollof — don't skimp.
2. In a heavy pot, heat the oil and fry the sliced onion until soft. Add the
   tomato paste and fry 3–4 minutes until it darkens and the oil turns red.
3. Add the reduced pepper base, curry, thyme, smoked paprika, bay, white pepper,
   and seasoning cube. Simmer 5–10 minutes until thick and glossy — the base
   should hold a line when you drag a spoon through it.
4. Stir in the rinsed rice until every grain is coated red. Add just enough stock
   to *barely* cover the rice — jollof is cooked drier than you think, so the
   grains stay separate.
5. Cover tightly (a layer of foil under the lid helps trap steam) and cook on the
   **lowest heat 25–30 minutes**. **Do not stir** — stirring makes it mushy.
6. For party-style flavor, in the last 5 minutes let the bottom catch *just
   slightly* on slightly raised heat to build the toasty *bottom-pot* aroma, then
   kill the heat and rest 10 minutes.
7. Fold gently with the browned chicken and serve — classically with fried
   plantain (*dodo*) and a simple coleslaw.

## The rice question

Nigerian party jollof is traditionally made with **parboiled long-grain rice**,
which is sturdy and forgiving and stays separate through the long cook. Ghanaian
jollof often uses fragrant **basmati or jasmine**. Both are "correct." Whatever
you use, rinse it well and go easy on the liquid.

## Make it yours

- **Ghanaian style:** aromatic rice, often a little ginger and shito (a dark
  pepper sauce) alongside.
- **Senegalese thieboudienne:** the original — built on fish, broken rice, and a
  medley of vegetables; a project dish worth seeking out.
- Vegetarian jollof is excellent — the pepper base carries it. Use vegetable
  stock and add a smoky note with extra smoked paprika.

::: {.callout-note}
## Who wins the Jollof War?
Diplomatically: whoever cooked the pot in front of you. Cook both, invite friends,
and let the table decide.
:::
